### Natural scene dataset

We used a natural scene dataset (Meyer et al., 2014), which contains 421 panoramic luminance-calibrated naturalistic two-dimensional pictures. Each picture has $927\times251$ pixels and subtends 360° horizontally and 97.4° vertically, so that the spatial resolution is ~0.30°/pixel. In our study, we used 1-dimensional images, which were single rows from the two-dimensional pictures. Therefore, there were $105671=421\times251$ images in the dataset. We refer to the two-dimensional scenes as pictures or photographs, and refer to the one-dimensional slices as images.

### Preprocessing photographs

To simulate the photoreceptors, we converted the luminance pictures into contrast pictures with a blurring step and contrast computation step.

First, to simulate the spatial resolution of the fly’s ommatidia, we blurred the original photograph (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), denoted by $I$, with a two-dimensional Gaussian filter $f_{blur}(x,y)$.

$$
I_{blur}(x,y)=I∗f_{blur}=\sumu,vI(x+u,y+v)f_{blur}(u_{,}v),
$$



$$
f_{blur}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2\pi\lambda_{blur}^{2}}exp⁡(−\frac{u^{2}+v^{2}}{2\lambda_{blur}^{2}}), u_{−}\lequ\lequ_{+}, v_{−}\leqv\leqv_{+}.
$$

where $∗$ denotes cross-correlation. The filter extends to $\pm3\lambda_{blur}$, that is $u_{+}=v_{+}=|u_{−}|=|v_{−}|=3\lambda_{blur}$, where $\lambda_{blur}$ is related to full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) by $\lambda_{blur}=\frac{FWHM_{blur}}{2\sqrt{2ln⁡2}}$, and we chose $FWHM_{blur}=5.3$° (Stavenga, 2003). The original pictures cover the full circular range horizontally, but only 97.4° vertically. When the range of the filter extended beyond the vertical boundary of the picture, we padded the picture by 'vertical reflection'. This reflection padding was also used when we calculated the local mean-luminance. In Figure 1B, where we demonstrated one example picture, we did not perform this blurring step in order to preserve high spatial acuity such that it is pleasing for human eyes.

Second, we converted the luminance signals in the blurred photograph to contrast signals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1CD) (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015),

$$
c(x,y)=\frac{I_{blur}(x,y)−I_{mean}(x,y)}{I_{mean}(x,y)},
$$



$$
I_{mean}(x,y)=I_{blur}∗f_{local-mean},
$$

where $cx,y$ is the contrast at each location $x,y$. $I_{mean}$ is the local mean luminance, which is the averaged luminance weighted by a two-dimensional Gaussian spatial filter $f_{local-mean}$. The length scale of $f_{local-mean}$ can be equivalently described by $\lambda_{local-mean}$ and $FWHM_{local-mean}$, where $\lambda_{local-mean}=\frac{FWHM_{local-mean}}{2\sqrt{2ln⁡2}}$. We swept $FWHM_{local-mean}$ from 10° to 75° (Figure 3—figure supplement 2ABC).

Alternatively, we also computed the local mean luminance over time instead of over space in Figure 3—figure supplement 2FG,

$$
I_{mean}(x,y,t)=\sumuI_{blur-time}(x,y,t)f_{local-mean-time}(t−u),
$$

where $I_{blur-time}(x,y,t)$ is the simulated naturalistic moving luminance signal (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015), and the local mean luminance was the averaged luminance signals over time, with the temporal filter $f_{local-mean-time}(t)=exp⁡(−t/\tau_{local-mean})$, where $f_{local-mean-time}(t)$ is normalized to have a sum of 1. We swept $\tau_{local-mean}$ from 10 ms to 500 ms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2FG).

Depending on the parameters in local mean computation, we had 20 natural scene datasets, including 14 datasets whose local mean luminance was computed statically and 6 dynamically. Unless specified, we used the natural scene dataset with contrast images preprocessed statically with $FWHM_{local-mean}=25$°.

### Eliminating the higher order structure of natural scene ensemble

We created a synthetic image dataset where we effectively preserved only the second-order structure of natural scenes ensemble and eliminated the higher-order structure. We viewed each 1D image as a random vector determined by $P_{natural}X,$where $X$ is a $n$-dimensional vector ($n=927$ for 927 pixels). The covariance matrix of $P_{natural}X$ determines the point variance and pairwise spatial correlations in natural scenes. We intended to construct a Gaussian distribution $P_{synthetic}X$ such that its covariance matrix is the same as $P_{natural}X$. In this way, the image ensemble sampled from $P_{synthetic}X$ will contain the same second-order statistics as the natural scene ensemble, but it would lack the higher order statistics present in the natural scene ensemble.

Because the pixels in images are horizontally translational invariant, the covariance matrix of $P_{natural}X$ is a circulant matrix and can be diagonalized by a discrete Fourier transform. Therefore, we constructed $P_{synthetic}X$ and generated the synthetic dataset in the frequency domain (Bialek, 2012). Operationally, we first performed a discrete Fourier transform (with fft function in Matlab v2018a, RRID:SCR_001622) on each one-dimensional image in the natural scene dataset and obtained its Fourier domain representation $y^{(i)}=(y_{k_{1}}^{i},y_{k_{2}}^{i},…,y_{k_{n}}^{(i)})$, where $(i)$ denotes the $i$th images, and $k_{n}$ denotes the $k_{n}$th Fourier component. We then calculated the average power of frequency $k_{n}$, denoted as $\sigma_{k_{n}}^{2}$, where $\sigma_{k_{n}}^{2}=\frac{1}{m}\sumimy_{k_{n}}^{(i)}y_{k_{n}}^{(i)}^{*}$, and $*$ denotes complex conjugation. At each frequency $k_{n}$, we built two Gaussian distributions $G_{ℜ}∼𝒩(0, \frac{\sigma_{k_{n}}^{2}}{2})$ and $G_{ℑ}∼𝒩(0, \frac{\sigma_{k_{n}}^{2}}{2})$. To generate one synthetic image, we sampled two real numbers from these two distributions as the real and imaginary part of Fourier component of the synthetic image at frequency $k_{n}$. In the end, we performed an inverse Fourier transform to the sampled Fourier components to gain a synthetic image in the spatial domain. In total, we generated 1000 high-order-structure-eliminated synthetic images, and refer to this synthetic image dataset to as the dataset in which higher order structure was eliminated.

### Computing and manipulating statistics of individual one-dimensional images

The natural scene dataset was comprised of an ensemble of heterogeneous images, and the statistics of different images can be drastically different from each other. Thus, we considered each one-dimensional image to have its own contrast distribution, $P_{pixel}^{(i)}(X)$, where $i$ indexes the image and the contrast of each pixel in an image as an independent sample of the random variable $X$. For each natural image, we computed its sample mean, sample variance, sample skewness, and sample kurtosis of pixels, and show the histogram of these statistics (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5B).

We generated $14=2+10+2$ synthetic image datasets to mimic various statistical properties of natural scenes (Table 2). These 14 datasets differ in three parameters: (1) the contrast range; (2) whether the contrast skewness was constrained; and (3) the specific value of the imposed skewness when the skewness was constrained. We conceptually justify this image synthesis method in Appendix 2, and here we focus on methodological details. For every image in the natural scene dataset, we generated a corresponding image in each synthetic image dataset. This involved two steps.

### Simulating naturalistic motion with natural scenes

To simulate the full-field motion signals induced by self-rotation in the natural environment, we rigidly translated images at various horizontal velocities (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015). For each trial, we randomly chose one 1-dimensional image from the dataset. We had 35 image datasets in total, including 20 natural scene datasets preprocessed with different parameters and 15 synthetic image datasets, we therefore built 35 naturalistic motion datasets, where all images were sampled from a particular image dataset in each motion dataset. We sampled the velocity in two ways. First, we sampled it from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and standard deviation of 114 °/s. This standard deviation is the measured standard deviation of the spontaneous rotational turning speed of freely walking flies. In Figure 3—figure supplement 1, we varied the standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution from 32 °/s to 512 °/s. Second, we selected an image velocity at discrete values ranging from 0 °/s to 1000 °/s with a 10 °/s interval. Given an image-velocity pair, we rigidly move this image with this velocity for one second. The temporal resolution is 60 Hz.

To eliminate any potential left-right asymmetry in naturalistic motion datasets, if we moved an image rightward at a certain speed, we always simulated a paired trial in which the same image was flipped horizontally and moved leftward with the same speed.

### Calculating the responses of different motion detectors to naturalistic motion signals

Our study concerns two motion detectors: the HRC and the measured kernels. For the HRC, we created an array of 54 overlapping HRC elementary motion detectors which extended 270° horizontally. We calculated the instantaneous HRCs’ outputs at the end of each trial and averaged them across space to get the model’s output $r_{HRC}$. For the measured kernels, we calculated the instantaneous output of the kernels at the end of each trial, including the second-order response, $r^{(2)},$ the third-order response, $r^{3}$, and the total response, $r=r^{(2)}+r^{(3)}$.

### Evaluating the performance of a motion detector

We denote the true velocity of the image as $v_{img}$ and the response of a motion detector as $v_{est}$. We assessed the accuracy of the motion estimation using two metrics. First, we measured the Pearson correlation $ρ$ between $v_{img}$ and $v_{est}$,

$$
ρ=\frac{cov(v_{est},v_{img})}{\sqrt{var(v_{est})}\sqrt{var(v_{img})}},
$$

where the variances and covariances are evaluated across any of the naturalistic motion datasets introduced above. To estimate the uncertainty in $ρ$ induced by finite sample sizes, we randomly separated all independently simulated trials into 10 groups, calculated the Pearson correlation for each group, and estimated the SEM of the Pearson correlation across the groups. Second, when the image velocity was sampled at discrete values, we measured the variance of $v_{est}$ conditional on each possible image velocity, $var(v_{est}|v_{img}=v_{0})$.

### Evaluating the improvement added by the third-order response

To evaluate how much improvement was added by the third-order response to the second-order response, we calculated the relative Pearson correlations: $improvement=\frac{ρ^{(2+3)}-ρ^{(2)}}{ρ^{(2)}}$. As in Evaluating the performance of a motion detector, to estimate the uncertainty induced by finite sample sizes, we separated all trials into 10 groups, calculated the Pearson correlation for each group, calculated the improvements in each group, and estimated the SEM of the improvements across the groups.

### Assessing the empirical weighting of the second-order and third-order responses

We modeled the image velocity as a linear combination of the second-order and third-order responses

$$
v_{img}=\alpha^{(2)}r^{(2)}+\alpha^{(3)}r^{(3)}+ϵ_{img},
$$

and estimated the optimal weighting coefficients, $(\alpha^^{(2)},\alpha^^{(3)})$, using ordinary least square regression. We calculated $ρ_{best}=\frac{cov(r_{best},v_{img})}{\sqrt{var(r_{best})}\sqrt{var(v_{img})}}$, where $r_{best}=\alpha^^{(2)}r^{(2)}+\alpha^^{(3)}r^{(3)}$. We computed the relative weighting coefficient as $w=\alpha^^{2}/\alpha^^{3}$.

### Calculating the residual of second-order response

The second-order response can be viewed as a function of the image velocity, as well as noise that depends on image structure:

$$
r^{(2)}=\beta^{(2)} v_{img}+ϵ^{(2)}.
$$

We estimated the noise term as

$$
ϵ^^{(2)}=r^{(2)}−\beta^^{(2)}v_{img},
$$

where $\beta^^{(2)}$ minimized the squared residual and $ϵ^^{(2)}$ denotes the estimated residual (noise).

Summary:

This paper takes a close look into the natural scene statistics that influence behavior. In particular, the work investigates the importance of second- and third-order stimulus correlations on motion sensing in flies. Second-order correlations have been emphasized in past work, and a few past studies have suggested that third-order correlations also contribute, but this work provides the first comprehensive treatment of the issue. The paper presents an analysis of fly behavioral responses to moving patterns based on rigid rotations of static natural scenes, either with fully natural statistics, or modified parametric stimuli that retain the skewness in the contrast distribution of natural scenes. Analysis of behavioral responses to these stimulus variants indicates that the fly uses third -order computations effectively to counter some of the systematic (and well-known) variations introduced by the second-order computations prescribed by canonical motion detection models. Both the experiments and the analysis are presented clearly, and the authors make a convincing case for their conclusion that the third-order term improves velocity estimation in natural scenes. The computational strategies discovered here likely extend to other visual systems. The stimulus construction algorithm developed here could also be used for other model systems and analyses.

Essential revisions:

1) As pointed out in the Discussion section, the Volterra kernel approximation represents a general and systematic approach to the identification of nonlinear systems (with practical caveats, as also mentioned). But there is also a more fundamental issue: Volterra kernels are essentially high dimensional polynomial approximations, and as such, although they are general, they are extremely inefficient in describing compressive nonlinearities (and biological systems are essentially always compressive in their typical range of operation). Motion estimation by correlation is a second-order Volterra operation, and therefore diverges quadratically. To counter that divergence, the system must somehow normalize the response to the contrast variance, such as in contrast normalization. And this is what seems to happen in biological motion detectors: It is well known that motion responses saturate as a function of contrast.

In this light, the finding that the third-order Volterra kernel improves velocity estimates can then be simply seen as a corollary of the fact that the third-order kernel is essentially a "fitting parameter" which is necessarily better than a fit to second-order. Alternatively, as noted in the paper, the third-order behavior could be due to more or less fixed asymmetries in processing, or even due to nonlinear behavior in early vision. Something along these lines was proposed by Bulthoff and Goetz (Bulthoff and Goetz, 1979) to explain a motion illusion in human and fly vision (and that should be cited in this paper).

These points should be addressed fully in the text of the paper, both in the Results and in the Discussion.

2) Response predictions and quantification. The kernel approach estimates behavioral responses, but the predictions are then compared directly to image velocity. Implicit in this (at least not clearly stated in the text of the manuscript) is that the behavior is linearly related to the image velocity – or at least that the two can be swapped in the analysis. It would be good to clarify this issue somewhere around the second paragraph of the subsection “Third-order kernel improve velocity estimation in moving natural scenes” where this analysis is described. At present, the text could be misread to indicate that image velocity is being estimated directly.

3) In the Discussion section:

- The interpretation of the main result (that the third-order term improves velocity estimation in natural scenes) feels a bit narrow; the authors should remedy that in the Discussion section.

- Ties to neural data need to be made a bit more extensive and detailed. Is there evidence to suggest that the kinds of optimal temporal filters derived here are found in the fly brain? Perhaps suggest a few other places to look, beyond what's already discussed (measuring T4/T5 kernels).

- Comment a bit more on the limitations/advantages of considering only rigid rotations applied to static natural or naturalistic scene stats. Perhaps also comment on using walking versus flight, and note that flies spend most of their time walking.

- Comment a bit more on the potential behavioral relevance of the magnitude of the effect of the improvement from third-order filter input to second-order processing.

- How prevalent is positive skewness in different natural scenes? Are there scenes/environments where one should expect more or less skewness? Would visual systems that operate in specialized niches be expected to have different nonlinearities in their motion processing as a result, or will all visual systems require some amount of compensation in their second-order motion detectors?

Title revisions:

Replace "perceptual" with "behavioral"

Suggested stylistic revisions:

The papers dives into contrast-polarity sensitivity right away, before sufficiently motivating the research approach as a whole. It also seems like this feature might require a more intuitive figure to explain the effect to the uninitiated. Perhaps a few more words about the behavioral advantages of this level of careful motion dissection would be useful.

In the last paragraph of the Introduction, it would be good to broaden the perspective a bit on how filters are usually computed in behavioral and neural recording experiments, how this relates to other filter-finding techniques, and what the third-order kernels might reveal. For a broad audience, it might also be good to remind the reader what a Volterra expansion is and add a note about adding kernels to the expansion versus static nonlinearities, along the lines discussed above.

Here and there the paper reads a bit too much like a travel journal – a few examples:

- The paragraphs in the subsection “The structure of natural scenes induces noise in second-order motion estimates” all have something like "We did something…Then we observed something, etc."

- The legend to Figure 3 is full of "we did this or that".

Consider revising the text to make the language just a bit more formal and deliberate in guiding the reader through the major scientific findings in the paper, by motivating and previewing the steps taken in this careful and thorough work.

results.result: Higher-order structure in natural scenes induces variability in canonical second-order motion estimates. The HRC model showed substantial variance when presented with natural scenes at fixed velocities, but this variance was markedly reduced when higher-order structure was eliminated from synthetic images while preserving second-order statistics.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 provide converging evidence from simulations showing that the HRC model exhibits velocity-dependent tuning with high variance across natural scenes (C49-C51), consistent with prior work (C52). The controlled experiment with synthetic images (C53-C54) directly demonstrates that eliminating higher-order structure reduces variance while preserving mean tuning, establishing causality (C55).

results.result: The study systematically characterized fly motion computation using Volterra series expansion, extending canonical second-order models with a third-order component to capture contrast-polarity-dependent processing. The Volterra framework allows rigorous separation of pairwise (second-order) and triplet (third-order) spatiotemporal correlation sensitivities.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 and C57-C66 establish the methodological approach with appropriate citations to prior work. The Volterra series is a well-established mathematical framework (C58, C61-C62), and its application to motion computation is properly justified (C63, C65-C66). The extension to third-order is methodologically sound and addresses a specific gap in prior work.

results.result: Second- and third-order Volterra kernels were successfully extracted from fly optomotor turning behavior using reverse-correlation with binary stochastic stimuli. The measured second-order kernel showed structure consistent with classical motion computation models, while the third-order kernel showed both positive and negative values.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C79 describe a well-established experimental and analytical approach with appropriate citations (C71-C75). The measured second-order kernel matches prior work (C78), providing validation. The third-order kernel measurement (C79) is novel but uses the same validated methodology. The high-throughput setup (C71) addresses the data requirements for higher-order kernel estimation.

results.result: The reliability of the third-order kernel was verified through statistical testing against null kernels and independent validation with glider stimuli. Many kernel elements were statistically significant (p<0.05), especially at short temporal delays, and most glider responses were quantitatively predicted by the kernel.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C121 provide two independent validation approaches. The null kernel analysis (C113-C115) establishes statistical significance with appropriate methodology. The glider validation (C116-C119) provides independent experimental confirmation with good quantitative agreement. Discrepancies are acknowledged and explained (C120). The convergence of evidence strongly supports kernel reliability (C121).

results.result: The third-order component improves velocity estimates by canceling image-induced variability in the second-order component. While the third-order response alone anti-correlates with velocity, when combined with the second-order response it improves motion estimation accuracy by ~25% through anticorrelation with second-order residuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 and C82-C99 present a coherent mechanistic explanation supported by data. The evaluation methodology is clearly described (C82, C87). The counterintuitive finding that third-order responses anti-correlate with velocity (C92) is explained by their role in canceling scene-dependent variability (C98-C99). The residual analysis (C98) provides direct evidence for this mechanism. The ~25% improvement is quantified with appropriate statistics.

results.result: The measured second- and third-order kernels are weighted near-optimally for naturalistic motion estimation. The improvement is robust to velocity distribution variance but depends on contrast computation parameters, with maximal utility at spatial and temporal scales matching fly visual processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C108 demonstrate optimization through parameter sweeps. The near-optimal weighting (C102) is established by comparison to fitted weights. Robustness to velocity variance (C103) is shown empirically. The dependence on contrast computation parameters (C104-C107) is systematically explored, and the peak performance at biologically realistic parameters (C108) provides strong support for functional optimization.

results.result: The study developed a method using maximum entropy distributions (MEDs) to generate synthetic images with precisely controlled contrast statistics. This addresses the challenge that natural image statistics are highly correlated, making it difficult to isolate effects of individual statistics.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C144 describe a methodologically sound approach to a real problem (C136-C137). The MED framework is well-established (C143) and appropriately applied. The method allows independent manipulation of mean, variance, and skewness (C140-C141), which is essential for testing the specific role of skewness. The approach is clearly described with appropriate mathematical justification (C142).

results.result: Positive image skewness is sufficient for the third-order signal to improve motion estimates. When only mean and variance were retained, the third-order response was near zero and provided no improvement. When skewness was added, the improvement was recovered. Systematic variation of skewness showed that positive skewness enables the third-order response to anticorrelate with second-order residuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C40 and C146-C154 provide strong causal evidence through controlled manipulation of image statistics. The comparison between images with and without skewness (C146-C147) isolates the critical variable. The systematic skewness sweep (C148-C149, C152) establishes a dose-response relationship. The mechanistic explanation through residual correlation (C152) is consistent with earlier findings. This is the key result linking natural scene statistics to functional benefit.

results.result: The second-order and third-order kernels share similar temporal structure, with peak sensitivity at short temporal delays. This similarity, confirmed by both direct comparison and singular value decomposition, suggests that pairwise and triplet correlation sensitivities may emerge from common physiological processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 present converging evidence from two independent analyses showing similar temporal structure. The finding is consistent with prior modeling work (C122). However, the inference about common physiological origin is speculative. The data support similar temporal tuning but do not directly establish shared mechanisms.

results.result: The measured third-order kernel shows qualitative agreement with theoretically optimized motion detectors in sign but differs quantitatively, particularly for correlations with large temporal delays. These differences could indicate biological suboptimalities or limitations of the optimization models.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C133 appropriately compare measured and theoretical kernels. The qualitative agreement (C128) provides support for optimization principles, while the quantitative differences (C129-C130) are honestly reported. The interpretation acknowledges multiple possible explanations (C131-C132) without overreaching. The conclusion about value for future work (C133) is reasonable.

results.result: The results motivate the hypothesis that fly turning responses reflect an internal velocity estimate specifically tailored for natural environments. A model fit to explain turning behavior successfully predicted image velocity, which was not guaranteed a priori.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C159 present a reasonable interpretation of the results. The observation that a behaviorally-fit model predicts velocity (C156-C157) is significant. However, this remains a hypothesis (C158) rather than direct proof. The inference about natural environment tailoring (C159) is supported by the skewness experiments but involves some interpretive leap from correlation to function.

results.result: The study used natural panoramic photographs converted to contrast signals and rigidly translated at various velocities to simulate naturalistic motion. This approach mimics rotational self-motion and is known to induce optomotor responses, though it is simpler than real motion through environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 describe standard methodology with appropriate citations (C41-C43, C45). The rationale for rigid translation is clearly explained (C46, C48), and limitations are acknowledged (C47). The preprocessing steps (C44) are standard. This is appropriate stimulus design for the research question, though the acknowledged simplification relative to natural motion is a limitation.

results.result: Many visual systems across the animal kingdom are likely to use asymmetric ON-OFF processing to improve motion estimation, since light-dark asymmetries are prevalent in natural environments and many visual systems exhibit ON-OFF asymmetric processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C7-C8, C160-C162 make broad generalizations based on the fly results. While the logic is reasonable (C7, C160-C161 cite relevant prior work), the leap from flies to "many animals" (C8, C162) is speculative. The prevalence of light-dark asymmetries (C7, C160) and ON-OFF asymmetric processing (C161) are established, but whether other animals use this specifically for motion estimation as flies do requires direct evidence.

results.result: Prior work established that visual systems may be tuned to natural scene statistics and that motion computation involves sensitivity to spatiotemporal correlations, including triplet correlations. However, previous studies had limitations: they measured only a few triplet correlations, did not assess utility in combination, and did not identify which natural scene statistics were sufficient for improvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C33 provide appropriate context and identify genuine gaps in prior work. The citations support the claims about established knowledge (C11-C12, C14-C17, C20, C25-C26) and limitations (C28-C29, C32-C33). The methodological principle about assessing correlations in combination (C30) is valid. This effectively motivates the current study.

results.result: Motion computation requires nonlinear transformations, and Volterra series provide a systematic polynomial approximation. However, polynomial descriptions can be inefficient for some nonlinearities like compressive saturation, and many terms may be needed. The approach has been successfully applied to model motion processing in flies and primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C59-C60, C64 accurately describe the Volterra approach with appropriate citations. The limitations (C59-C60) are honestly stated. The prior applications (C64) support the validity of the approach. This provides appropriate methodological context without overstating the method's capabilities.

results.result: The study used optomotor turning responses as a proxy for velocity estimates and evaluated performance using Pearson correlation coefficients. The velocity distribution was chosen to match spontaneous turning in walking flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81, C83, C85, C88-C89 describe standard methodology with appropriate justification. The hypothesis that turning reflects velocity estimation (C81) is supported by prior work. The choice of velocity distribution (C83) is well-justified. The Pearson correlation metric (C88-C89) is appropriate for the linear relationship assumed. These are reasonable methodological choices.

results.result: The third-order kernel was visualized using impulse response format, showing that behavioral consequences of triplet correlations last almost a second and that different triplet correlations vary significantly in direction and magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 describe a visualization approach that aids interpretation. The impulse response concept (C109-C110) is standard in systems theory. The observations about temporal extent (C111) and variability (C112) are descriptive results from the data. This is appropriate data presentation but represents analysis/visualization rather than a primary finding.

results.result: Flies combine local pairwise and triplet correlations to reduce variability in motion estimates across natural scenes, with triplet correlations being useful only when images have light-dark asymmetries that mimic natural ones, suggesting that asymmetric ON-OFF processing is tuned to natural scene statistics.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 summarize the main findings accurately. C4 is supported by the kernel measurements and performance analysis. C5 is supported by the synthetic image experiments. C6 is a reasonable inference from C5. These claims effectively summarize the paper's core contributions.

results.result: The second-order response is influenced by both image velocity and scene structure, and reducing scene-dependent variability in the second-order estimate is one way to improve accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide interpretive context for understanding the main results. C95 is a logical observation. C96 refers back to earlier simulations. C97 is a reasonable inference about how to improve performance. These claims help explain the counterintuitive finding about third-order responses.

results.result: Synthetic images with retained skewness maintained naturalistic light-dark asymmetries. When images were negatively skewed, the third-order response correlated with velocity but positively correlated with second-order residuals, decreasing overall performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C145, C150-C151 describe results from the skewness manipulation experiments. C145 is a logical statement about what skewness represents. C150-C151 show that the sign of skewness matters, with negative skewness producing the opposite effect. This demonstrates specificity and strengthens the causal argument about positive skewness.
